head.prose: **Goal:** a health system that ensures the right number and skill mix of trained health and care personnel with the right skills are in the right place at the right time to meet population health needs, and a health workforce whose members — across both regulated professions and non-licensed or community cadres — are individually identifiable and verifiable (**Sub-goal 2.1**), equitably deployed and retained where they are needed (**Sub-goal 2.2**), paid reliably and on time in compliance with labour rights (**Sub-goal 2.3**), supported to maintain and extend their competencies across the course of their careers (**Sub-goal 2.4**), and backed by trustworthy registration and authorisation status that safeguards patient safety, public accountability, and worker privacy (**Sub-goal 2.5**).

base.prose: **What the health system needs to be able to do:** the system needs to know who its health workers are and what each is qualified and authorised to do, holding an authoritative record of identity, occupational classification, professional registration, and licensing status that clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently rely on. It needs to see where workers are deployed and where shortages persist, so that staffing can be planned against population need rather than inferred from incomplete or paper-based records. And it needs to pay workers reliably, and to track the education, credentialing, and supervision through which competence is established and renewed over time.

It needs to see where workers are deployed and where shortages persist, so that staffing can be planned against population need rather than inferred from incomplete or paper-based records. And it needs to pay workers reliably, and to track the education, credentialing, and supervision through which competence is established and renewed over time.

head.prose: **What the health system needs to be able to do:** the system needs to know who all of its health and care workers are and what each is qualified and authorised to do — covering statutory licensed practitioners overseen by health practitioner regulators as well as non-regulated cadres, community health workers, multiskilled personnel, provisional registrants, students and trainees, and volunteers authorised through national programme or employer mechanisms where formal licensure or foundational national identity is absent. It must hold an authoritative reference record of workforce identity, occupational and role classification, educational qualifications, and professional registration or authorisation status that clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can rely on, while explicitly separating verified registration and qualifications from current clinical competence, task-specific authorisation, facility-level clinical privileging, fitness to practise, and authorised scope of practice (which depend on ongoing clinical governance, credential verification, supervision, competence assessment, and regulatory standing). To align with the WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and the health labour market framework, it needs to distinguish among workers who are *licensed to practise*, *professionally active*, and *practising*, and enable national and subnational planners and policymakers to track active workforce capacity, skill mix, and subnational distribution so that imbalances in the health labour market can be identified and minimised. Rather than inferring staffing adequacy from worker location and facility affiliation alone, the system needs analytical and planning capabilities that combine workforce deployment, contract/full-time equivalent (FTE) capacity, and scope of practice with catchment population need, service demand, workload, facility readiness, and infrastructure data, alongside external statistical and administrative sources of varying digital maturity (such as population censuses, labour force surveys, and national pension or social-security schemes). Finally, it needs to pay workers reliably and uphold labour rights (including salary, leave, pension, accreditation, and continuing professional development) by connecting verified workforce identity and active deployment records with operational HR, contract, attendance, public financial management, payroll, and learning systems — keeping detailed HR administrative actions, extended leaves, pay calculations, and course-level learning records inside those operational systems while enforcing strict compliance with data confidentiality and privacy laws, purpose-limited dataset sharing, worker transparency, and avenues for correction and appeal.

Its most significant shared components are the Health Workforce Registry it centres on — itself a core foundational registry that other health goals also rely on — supported by the terminology service for occupational and qualification coding and the facility registry for linking workers to their sites of practice and mapping deployment, all resting on foundational-DPI identity, trust, payments, and single sign-on services. The workforce goal introduces no new DPI-H component; the operational systems that act on the registry — digital payroll, human-resource information systems, and learning-management and training-tracking applications — sit outside DPI-H and consume it rather than being defined by it.

head.prose:
**How to read the mapping:** the spreadsheet and capability summary that follow trace each workforce sub-goal (`2.1`–`2.5`) through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the shared DPI-H components, foundational-DPI dependencies, and operational workforce-management systems required to realise the goal, noting where shared components are reused across other goals:

- **Shared DPI-H reference components versus operational workforce systems:** the mapping centres on three shared DPI-H components — the **Health Workforce Registry** (a core foundational registry reused across clinical care, surveillance, supply chain, and health financing), the **Health Facility Registry**, and the **Terminology Service** — resting on foundational-DPI identity, trust/verifiable credentials, payment rails, data exchange, and single sign-on services. However, these shared registries alone cannot deliver Goal 2 without the operational systems that consume and update them: Human Resources for Health Information Systems (HRHIS) and employer HRIS, civil-service and facility payroll, contract management, public financial management (PFM), time and attendance, shift scheduling, deployment management, professional regulatory council platforms, clinical privileging and supervision tools, pre-service education and accreditation systems, learning-management systems (LMS), and workforce-planning and health labour market modelling applications. In particular, foundational payment DPI provides disbursement rails but does not determine employment validity, salary calculation, attendance, deductions, payment authorisation, or budget availability (which belong to HR, contract, attendance, payroll, and PFM systems); similarly, the Health Workforce Registry holds authoritative qualification and high-level continuing professional development (CPD) compliance references, whereas detailed learning activities, curricula, supervision logs, and competency assessments belong to LMS, education, and accreditation systems.
- **Care-services discovery model and dual national/international terminology governance:** linking workforce and service delivery requires more than joining a worker identifier to a facility identifier. The mapping aligns the Health Workforce Registry, Health Facility Registry, and Terminology Service with a full care-services discovery model — such as the IHE Mobile Care Services Discovery (mCSD) profile — capturing the distinct relationships among *Organisation* (employer, regulator, or provider organisation), *Practitioner* (regulated or non-regulated worker), *PractitionerRole* (role, specialty, authorised scope of practice, task-sharing authority, contract/FTE basis, and active period), *Location / Facility*, and *HealthcareService*. Because international classifications alone cannot represent country-specific cadres, multiskilled workers, community health work, task sharing, or local scope of practice, the Terminology Service governs national occupation, role, specialty, credential, and scope-of-practice vocabularies separately and maintains structured mappings to international classifications — **ISCO-08** (WHO health worker classification framework) for occupations and **ISCED** (International Standard Classification of Education) for educational qualifications — alongside interoperability with multi-source national data (regulatory registers, censuses, labour force surveys, and pension schemes) to populate NHWA indicators across *licensed to practise*, *professionally active*, and *practising* statuses.
- **Boundary of registry data, privacy compliance, and purpose-limited reuse:** the Health Workforce Registry must comply with national data confidentiality, privacy, and data-protection laws. Detailed HR administrative records (such as extended leaves of absence, internal administrative or disciplinary proceedings, performance appraisals, and pay/deduction schedules) are held in employer HRIS and payroll systems; the shared registry records only the resulting high-level operational deployment status and regulator-issued licence/authorisation status. To prevent unnecessary exposure of personal residential addresses, nationality, disciplinary histories, salary details, or employment terms during payroll validation or workforce planning, the architecture enforces purpose-specific datasets and role-based access controls, provides de-identified or aggregated datasets for workforce planning and NHWA reporting, and gives health workers audit transparency into access to their records together with formal mechanisms for correction and appeal.
- **Suggested phased implementation sequence:** countries can sequence these capabilities progressively as infrastructure matures: (1) *Phase 1 — Governed workforce identity, classification, and registration/authorisation status*, establishing unique workforce identifiers across licensed and non-licensed/CHW cadres, governed national role and qualification terminology mapped to ISCO-08 and ISCED, authoritative registration/authorisation status, and privacy, correction, and appeal controls; (2) *Phase 2 — Organisational affiliations and mCSD care-services discovery*, linking Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organisation, Facility/Location, and HealthcareService records with NHWA activity statuses (*licensed to practise*, *professionally active*, *practising*) and contract/FTE data; (3) *Phase 3 — Workforce planning analytics, LMS/CPD integration, and payroll/HR validation*, combining aggregated workforce, facility, service-demand, workload, catchment-population, and external statistical/pension data for shortage mapping, connecting LMS/accreditation systems for CPD compliance, and integrating HRIS, attendance, PFM, and payroll systems for payee validation and NHWA compensation reporting; and (4) *Phase 4 — Cross-border and regional credential verification and mobility reporting*, enabling bilateral or regional verification of credentials and ethical recruitment monitoring.

head.prose:
The second goal is **supporting a capable, well-distributed health workforce**. This goal combines the health-system perspective — ensuring that the right number and skill mix of trained health and care personnel with the right skills are in the right place at the right time to meet population health needs — with the health-worker perspective, in which every health and care worker is individually identifiable and verifiable, equitably deployed where needed, paid reliably and on time, and supported to maintain and extend their competencies across the course of their career while upholding labour rights (including accreditation, continuing professional development, fair remuneration, leave, and pension protection). At national and subnational levels, it gives health-system planners and policymakers the information needed to track active workforce capacity, monitor and correct imbalances across the health labour market, ensure equitable distribution across geographic areas, facility types, and skill mixes, and strengthen workforce and health-service planning, distribution, and retention. In alignment with the WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and the health labour market framework, the architecture distinguishes between personnel who are *licensed to practise*, *professionally active*, and *practising*, and covers both statutory licensed professionals regulated by health practitioner regulators and non-licensed or community health and care cadres (including community health workers, allied and auxiliary staff, multiskilled workers, provisional registrants, trainees, and volunteers).

Achieving this goal requires a coordinated system approach in which shared DPI-H reference infrastructure works alongside operational workforce, education, and financial systems as well as external statistical and administrative data sources of varying digital maturity and non-health primary purposes (such as population censuses and labour force surveys conducted by national statistical offices, civil-service registers, and national pension or social-security schemes). Within DPI-H, an authoritative **Health Workforce Registry** — governed in strict compliance with national data confidentiality, privacy, and data-protection laws and purpose-limited data minimisation — connects with foundational identification systems where available, health practitioner regulators, educational qualification records, the **Health Facility Registry** (using care-services discovery patterns that relate organisations, facilities, locations, healthcare services, and practitioner roles), and the **Terminology Service** (governing national occupation, role, specialty, credential, and scope-of-practice vocabularies mapped to international classifications such as ISCO-08 and ISCED). The shared registry separates verified educational qualifications and regulatory registration from current clinical competence, task-specific authorisation, facility privileging, fitness to practise, and scope of practice, and records only high-level activity, deployment, and regulatory licence status; detailed human-resource administrative records (such as extended leaves of absence, internal administrative or disciplinary actions, attendance, salary calculations, deductions, and pension administration) and detailed learning records remain in operational human-resource information systems (HRIS/HRHIS), payroll and public financial management systems, and learning-management systems (LMS).

Across these shared and operational capabilities, the goal is structured around five mutually reinforcing sub-goals:

- **Sub-goal 2.1 — Identity and verifiable credentials established:** establishing governed workforce identity, educational qualifications (classified using ISCED), and professional registration, licensing, or alternative programme/employer authorisation for every regulated and non-regulated health and care worker, linked with health practitioner regulators, foundational identification systems, and HR/payroll systems while separating registration from clinical privileging, current competence, and scope of practice.
- **Sub-goal 2.2 — Equitable deployment, distribution, and shortage mapping enabled:** providing high-quality workforce data for planning, deployment, retention, and shortage mapping by combining mCSD-aligned practitioner-role, organisation, facility, and service affiliations (including NHWA activity status and full-time equivalent capacity) with catchment population need, service demand, workload, facility infrastructure, and external labour-market data sources.
- **Sub-goal 2.3 — Reliable and timely remuneration:** linking verified workforce identity and active deployment references in the Health Workforce Registry with operational HRIS, contract, attendance, payment-authorisation, public financial management, and payroll systems over foundational payment DPI rails, while informing NHWA indicators on compensation expenditure, entry-level wages and salaries, and pay gaps.
- **Sub-goal 2.4 — Continuous competency and career development:** tracking qualifications, continuing professional development (CPD) compliance, specialization, and licence renewal across a worker's career by linking authoritative qualification and compliance references in the Health Workforce Registry with operational LMS, pre-service education, accreditation, and clinical supervision systems.
- **Sub-goal 2.5 — Safety, accountability, and privacy-preserving governance:** enabling patients, health facilities, payers, and health practitioner regulators to verify that a worker's registration, licence, or authorisation status is accurate and current — protecting against payroll fraud and uncredentialed care — while enforcing purpose-specific access controls, de-identified or aggregated planning views, worker transparency, and rights of correction and appeal.

The second goal is supporting a capable, well-distributed health workforce. This goal combines the health-system perspective — ensuring that the right number and skill mix of trained health and care personnel with the right skills are in the right place at the right time to meet population health needs — with the health-worker perspective, in which every health and care worker is individually identifiable and verifiable, equitably deployed where needed, paid reliably and on time, and supported to maintain and extend their competencies across the course of their career while upholding labour rights (including accreditation, continuing professional development, fair remuneration, leave, and pension protection). At national and subnational levels, it gives health-system planners and policymakers the information needed to track active workforce capacity, monitor and correct imbalances across the health labour market, ensure equitable distribution across geographic areas, facility types, and skill mixes, and strengthen workforce and health-service planning, distribution, and retention. In alignment with the WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and the health labour market framework, the architecture distinguishes between personnel who are licensed to practise, professionally active, and practising, and covers both statutory licensed professionals regulated by health practitioner regulators and non-licensed or community health and care cadres (including community health workers, allied and auxiliary staff, multiskilled workers, provisional registrants, trainees, and volunteers).

Achieving this goal requires a coordinated system approach in which shared DPI-H reference infrastructure works alongside operational workforce, education, and financial systems as well as external statistical and administrative data sources of varying digital maturity and non-health primary purposes (such as population censuses and labour force surveys conducted by national statistical offices, civil-service registers, and national pension or social-security schemes). Within DPI-H, an authoritative Health Workforce Registry — governed in strict compliance with national data confidentiality, privacy, and data-protection laws and purpose-limited data minimisation — connects with foundational identification systems where available, health practitioner regulators, educational qualification records, the Health Facility Registry (using care-services discovery patterns that relate organisations, facilities, locations, healthcare services, and practitioner roles), and the Terminology Service (governing national occupation, role, specialty, credential, and scope-of-practice vocabularies mapped to international classifications such as ISCO-08 and ISCED). The shared registry separates verified educational qualifications and regulatory registration from current clinical competence, task-specific authorisation, facility privileging, fitness to practise, and scope of practice, and records only high-level activity, deployment, and regulatory licence status; detailed human-resource administrative records (such as extended leaves of absence, internal administrative or disciplinary actions, attendance, salary calculations, deductions, and pension administration) and detailed learning records remain in operational human-resource information systems (HRIS/HRHIS), payroll and public financial management systems, and learning-management systems (LMS).

Across these shared and operational capabilities, the goal is structured around five mutually reinforcing sub-goals:

  • Sub-goal 2.1 — Identity and verifiable credentials established: establishing governed workforce identity, educational qualifications (classified using ISCED), and professional registration, licensing, or alternative programme/employer authorisation for every regulated and non-regulated health and care worker, linked with health practitioner regulators, foundational identification systems, and HR/payroll systems while separating registration from clinical privileging, current competence, and scope of practice.
  • Sub-goal 2.2 — Equitable deployment, distribution, and shortage mapping enabled: providing high-quality workforce data for planning, deployment, retention, and shortage mapping by combining mCSD-aligned practitioner-role, organisation, facility, and service affiliations (including NHWA activity status and full-time equivalent capacity) with catchment population need, service demand, workload, facility infrastructure, and external labour-market data sources.
  • Sub-goal 2.3 — Reliable and timely remuneration: linking verified workforce identity and active deployment references in the Health Workforce Registry with operational HRIS, contract, attendance, payment-authorisation, public financial management, and payroll systems over foundational payment DPI rails, while informing NHWA indicators on compensation expenditure, entry-level wages and salaries, and pay gaps.
  • Sub-goal 2.4 — Continuous competency and career development: tracking qualifications, continuing professional development (CPD) compliance, specialization, and licence renewal across a worker's career by linking authoritative qualification and compliance references in the Health Workforce Registry with operational LMS, pre-service education, accreditation, and clinical supervision systems.
  • Sub-goal 2.5 — Safety, accountability, and privacy-preserving governance: enabling patients, health facilities, payers, and health practitioner regulators to verify that a worker's registration, licence, or authorisation status is accurate and current — protecting against payroll fraud and uncredentialed care — while enforcing purpose-specific access controls, de-identified or aggregated planning views, worker transparency, and rights of correction and appeal.
